entry.title: feat: pragmatic functions verify against the paradigm, and Dari keeps…
entry.content:
feat: pragmatic functions verify against the paradigm, and Dari keeps its phrases

Ports the substantive half of riera 29b5e0d: `pragmaticFunctions` members are
inflected surface forms by construction - what a person says, not citation
forms - and `direct()` has required a lemma-identical hit since a256cc7, so the
whole category was unverifiable. It is now checked against the language's own
paradigm via `text.generatedFormsByKey`.

That is not a relaxation. `direct()`'s rule exists because the resolver's
morphological fallback can land on an unrelated lexeme (`sec` "dry" -> `seure`
"to sit"); asking the paradigm keeps exactly that guard, since the accident is
not a form the entry generates. Verified in riera by planting invented words:
still reported as gaps.

With it, the three Dari phrases the previous commit had to compromise on -
امکان ندارد, لطفاً تکرار کنید, می‌خواهی بیایی - verify as written, so the draft's
original wording is restored and the two lemma substitutions are reverted. prs
now has no pragmatic gaps at all; the 4 that remain are the pre-existing
semanticFields ones (خاکی, گرمی, سردی), untouched here.

Also drops the dead `CA_SENTENCES` block and Catalan phrase case this repo
inherited from the fork - the mirror of what riera did for Dari.

That mirror is the lesson now written into port.sh: a commit whose point is
removing the *other* language's dead data must not be cherry-picked. Doing it
deleted darya's own Dari sentences and left it testing Catalan it does not
ship, caught by reading the diff rather than the gate, which stayed green
because the file still had sentences in it - just the wrong language's.
port.sh in this repo was also still the pre-fix version; synced from riera.

Lexicon audited: 0 removed, 0 new, 0 repointed, nothing outside `tags`.
Gate: pnpm gate 0, 533 tests, validate:content 0.

entry.title: feat: beginners can ask, offer, agree and repair - not just describe
entry.content:
feat: beginners can ask, offer, agree and repair - not just describe

Recovers the pedagogy work from `beginner-functions` (f8dcfed, 3 Aug), which
never merged and could not be merged: the branch predates the fork and touched
both languages' lexicons, and a month of lexicon changes had moved underneath
it. A raw merge hit nine conflicts in a 3.5 MB JSON - and its two new entries
carried ids lx-6158 and lx-6160, which now belong to شکم and سبزی. Merging it
would have duplicated ids or repointed real learner progress. Applied
semantically instead, through the repo's own tooling.

What the branch found still stands: `verbFunctions` groups verbs by SEMANTIC
DOMAIN and nothing in the spec ever required a learner be able to ask for
something, ask permission, offer, accept, agree, suggest or repair a
misunderstanding. For a product pitched on holding a conversation, those are
the first moves. `pragmaticFunctions` adds them, modelled on the Council of
Europe Threshold / PCIC A1-A2 inventories, in the register people actually use
in Kabul - قبول/موافقم to agree, اجازه to ask permission.

Both of its silent-failure fixes are carried over, and both matter more than
the content:

  * readSpec/specWords only read the four categories they were written for, so
    a new one was dropped on the floor and the run reported a clean "no gaps"
    for requirements nothing had checked. `assertKnownCategories` now exits
    non-zero on any category the checker cannot verify. Verified by planting an
    unknown category: the run stops with that message instead of printing a gap
    report.
  * `usable()` and tag-beginner-core split phrases on whitespace, which cannot
    decompose Catalan apostrophation (`d'acord`). Both now use the production
    tokenizer. The effect here is visible: tagging drops سو, بالیدن, خزیدن, کل
    and شک, none of which the spec requires - سو, کل and شک are fragments of
    words it does require (سوم, کلید, تشکر). The old split was over-tagging.

Three of the draft's spec entries no longer hold. They name inflected forms,
and `direct()` has required a lemma-identical hit since a256cc7 (11 Aug) so a
requirement cannot be met by a word one derivation removed - the draft was
measured against the laxer checker, which is why it reported no gaps. Two were
replaced by the content lemma each is built on (امکان ندارد -> امکان,
لطفاً تکرار کنید -> تکرار); می‌خواهی بیایی was dropped, both its verbs already
being covered in the same block.

Lexicon: two entries added via add-lexicon-entries.ts, which assigns fresh ids
(lx-6222 لحظه, lx-6223 موافق). اجازه was already added independently this month
as lx-6181. Audited: 0 entries removed, 0 ids repointed, tagging touched only
the `tags` field.

Gates: pnpm gate 0, 533 tests (14 new sentences), validate:content 0,
verify-beginner-core back to its pre-existing 4 gaps - none introduced here.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: docs: this repo is one product now, and says how to port from the other
entry.content:
docs: this repo is one product now, and says how to port from the other

CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md still described one codebase building two apps. Two of
the five hard-won rules were about hazards the split removed - the
`for L in ca prs` loop, and `content/active` being shared state that could be
flipped under a running dev server. Left as-is they would send someone looking
for a language that is not here.

Rewritten as what is true now, keeping what the split did not change: silent
failures, never renumber a lexicon entry, comments are load-bearing, and the
whole cost section - the free-tier provider chain is shared by BOTH products, so
that budget is tighter after the split, not looser.

Adds "Porting from the sibling" and scripts/port.sh. The habit it asks for is
the one that decides whether this fork was worth doing: keep shared changes in
their own commit, separate from language-specific ones. Before the split a
single commit routinely touched nine shared files plus both languages prompts;
split in two, the shared half is one cherry-pick.

fix: the default language comes from content/, not from a literal "prs"

The first green typecheck in this repo still failed twelve test files with a
module resolution error, because `DEFAULT_LANG = "prs"` was written down in six
places outside the profile registry: vitest.config.ts, scripts/content-path.ts,

of them sent the run looking for `content/prs`.

The fork simulation missed all six because it ran the gate with

cannot default to a language it does not ship. Tests compare against

entry.title: fix: the service worker no longer hardcodes one product's name
entry.content:
fix: the service worker no longer hardcodes one product's name

public/sw.js is static and cannot import the language profile, so its push
notification fallback was the literal "Darya" - shipped unchanged to the
Catalan build, where the product is Riera.

Latent rather than active: all three senders (cron reminders, chat notify, push
test) always set a title, so the fallback never fires today. That is precisely
why it survived - and why the next sender that forgets a title would have shown
Catalan learners the wrong product name.

Reads `short_name` from the web manifest instead, which already comes from
`profile.brand.appName`. One copy of this file stays correct for both brands,
so the fork does not have to diverge here.

Found by fingerprinting an actual Catalan build rather than reading the code:
24 files in `.next` contained "Riera" and 17 contained "Darya". Most of the 17
are the `prs` profile, which is bundled into both builds by design and which
the fork removes on its own; sw.js was the one that the fork would not have
fixed by itself.

entry.title: test: a script that proves the tree can still be split
entry.content:
test: a script that proves the tree can still be split

Grepping for `import ".../lang/<code>/..."` finds module coupling and misses
everything that names a language as data. Six test files hardcoded
`["ca", "prs"]` and then read `content/<lang>/`; the shared tree was green
throughout, because both languages were there. Only removing one showed it, and
then four whole test files failed to load rather than reporting anything.

So the check is the removal. `scripts/simulate-fork.sh` deletes one language in
place, runs typecheck, lint, test and validate:content, and puts the tree back
from a snapshot plus `git checkout content/`. It refuses to start if content/ is
dirty, since it restores that from git.

Both directions pass today. Run it after touching src/lib/lang, scripts/, or any
test that loops over languages.

entry.title: refactor: tests read the language list from the registry, not a literal
entry.content:
refactor: tests read the language list from the registry, not a literal

Simulating each fork - deleting one language and running the gate - found a
class the import grep could not: tests that name a language as *data* rather
than importing its module. Six files hardcoded `["ca", "prs"]` and then read
`content/<lang>/`, so in a single-language build four of them failed to load at
all, reporting an import error instead of anything about the content.

`REGISTERED_LANGS` now comes from the profile registry, which is the only thing
that actually knows what a build carries. cefr, levels, teachability,
word-selection and text-pool loop over it.

Two could not be folded into a loop and say so instead:

  * freq-integrity - prs must match its TSV exactly while ca carries a measured,
    capped drift. Merging them would assert the weaker of the two, so each
    stands down when its language is absent.
  * the alphabet route guard - it imports the route it guards, and a language
    with no script course deletes that tree. `describe.skipIf` does not help:
    tsc resolves the path even when the test never runs. Moved next to the
    route as `app/(app)/alphabet/layout.test.ts`, so it is deleted with the
    feature it belongs to.

capabilities.test.ts also pinned `PROFILES.prs` / `PROFILES.ca` directly, which
is a type error rather than a skipped test once the registry holds one language;
the expectations are now a table keyed by code, with a check that every
registered language has one.

Both forks were then simulated end to end and pass the whole gate:

  Riera (ca only)  typecheck 0, lint 0, 622 tests, validate 0
  Darya (prs only) typecheck 0, lint 0, 519 tests, validate 0

Shared tree unchanged: typecheck 0, lint 0, ca 836, prs 828, validate 0/0.

entry.title: refactor: shared scripts and tests read the language from the registry
entry.content:
refactor: shared scripts and tests read the language from the registry

Six shared files imported `lang/ca/*` and `lang/prs/*` by path and dispatched on
`lang === "ca"`. Two of them run inside `pnpm test`, so they would break the
default suite in both forks, not just an opt-in script.

All of them wanted normalize / matchKey / tokenize / buildIndex, which are
already on `profile.text` - the dual imports were the only reason these files
named a language at all.

  * beginner-expressible.test.ts - sentences keyed by code, tokenizer and index
    from the profile; runs whichever languages are registered.
  * mine-pairings.test.ts - its fixtures are Catalan words, so it is a Catalan
    test and now says so: reads the profile from the registry and skips when
    Catalan is absent, instead of failing to resolve an import. Equivalent Dari
    fixtures were never written; skipping makes that visible rather than
    pretending the miner is covered.
  * author-brief.manual.test.ts - the per-language `await import(".../surface
    .ts")` branches moved to `text.inflectionHint`. Dynamic imports are still
    resolved by tsc, so this failed `typecheck`, not just runtime.
  * build-frequency, verify-beginner-core, tag-beginner-core,
    audit-lexicon-coverage - mechanical: one `langProfile(lang).text`.
    audit-lexicon-coverage also imported ZWNJ for a single character class that
    already mixed Dari's ZWNJ with Catalan's apostrophes; inlined as ‌ with
    a note, since neither language's separators occur in the other's text.

Verified by output rather than by reading: verify-beginner-core and
audit-lexicon-coverage produce byte-identical output in both languages against
the pre-change code (including prs verify-beginner-core still exiting 1 on its
pre-existing content condition), and tag-beginner-core leaves the lexicons
untouched in both. build-frequency was NOT run - it regenerates committed TSVs
from the corpora and another session changed that script an hour ago; its edit
is the same mechanical substitution as the three that were proven identical.

`inflectionHint` had no test at all, and a brief silently missing every hint
still renders - covered now, one case per part of speech per language.

Gates: typecheck 0, lint 0, test ca 835 / prs 827, validate 0/0.

entry.title: refactor: audit-homographs asks the profile for generated surfaces
entry.content:
refactor: audit-homographs asks the profile for generated surfaces

The homograph audit runs inside `pnpm validate:content` - validate-content.ts
imports `auditHomographs` - so decoupling the gate in the previous commit was
incomplete while the audit itself imported `lang/ca/lexicon-index.ts` and
`lang/prs/lexicon-index.ts`. Either fork deletes one and the shared content gate
stops compiling through its own dependency.

`ambiguousSurfacesCa` and `ambiguousSurfacesPrs` were the same function twice.
The only real difference was how each enumerated generated surfaces: Catalan
folded `generatedSurfacesOf` per entry, Dari read `buildGeneratedForms`, which
returns an already-folded map. That is now one `LanguageText` method,
`generatedFormsByKey`, and one `ambiguousSurfaces` here.

Behaviour is unchanged, and this is the check that had to prove it rather than
be reasoned about: `pnpm validate:content` output is byte-identical in both
languages, including the audit's own counts - ca 180 ambiguous surfaces / 256
used in seed texts, prs 43 / 23. Those numbers are what would move if the
enumeration or the first-write-wins precedence had shifted.

Gates: typecheck 0, lint 0, test ca 827 / prs 819.

entry.title: refactor: let the language answer what a bad verb headword is
entry.content:
refactor: let the language answer what a bad verb headword is

`scripts/validate-content.ts` is the content gate for every language, and it
was the one file that could not survive a per-language repo: it imported
`verbSpec` from lang/ca/lexicon-index.ts and `ZWNJ` from lang/prs/normalize.ts
and dispatched on `lang === "ca"` / `lang === "prs"`. Either fork deletes one of
those directories, so either fork fails to compile its own content gate.

Replace the three branches with one call to a new `LanguageText`
method, `verbHeadwordProblem(normalized)`, which returns why an entry cannot be
a verb headword or null. Same question in both languages - can the engine
resolve this entry's forms? - with a wholly language-specific answer, so it
belongs on the profile next to normalize/matchKey/tokenize/buildIndex.

Dari reuses `derivePastStem` for the infinitive test rather than repeating
/(دن|تن)$/, so the validator and the conjugator cannot drift apart on what an
infinitive is.

The exemption list moved too, and that turned out to matter. It was a set of
lexeme ids (lx-0010, lx-0287, lx-0290) in the shared script. All three ids also
exist in the Catalan lexicon - `ens`, `fins després`, `llet` - so once the check
stopped being gated on `lang === "prs"`, those ids would have exempted Catalan
entries as well. None is a verb today, so nothing was actually wrong; it was an
accident, not a guarantee. Keyed on the Dari word inside the Dari profile, it
cannot reach another language at all. Verified: with `llet` (lx-0290) forced to
pos="verb", the gate now reports it; under the id-keyed version it was silent.

Verified both rules end to end, not just as units: each language's lexicon was
temporarily given a bad verb entry, the gate reported it, and the lexicon was
restored and confirmed byte-identical. `verb-headword.test.ts` pins the reject
cases, which are the ones "All content valid" cannot witness; it reads its cases
from a table keyed by language code and runs only the codes registered, so it
needs no edit when a deployment carries one language.

Gates: typecheck 0, lint 0, test ca 827 passed / prs 819 passed, validate 0/0.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: chore: delete 38 tracked throwaway files and fix .env.example drift
entry.content:
chore: delete 38 tracked throwaway files and fix .env.example drift

`pnpm lint` was failing on main, and every one of the 8 errors was in a file
nobody imports: scripts/dump-texts.js, scripts/temp-extract-remaining.test.ts
(a "temp-" file that ran inside the default suite), and test-gen.ts. Around
them sat ~35 more committed one-off probes - gen_*.py, generate_*.py,
*_audit.md, curl.html, next.log, temp-schedule-*.txt, validation_output.txt.

Checked every one for inbound references from src, scripts, docs, content and
the configs before removing: none. lint goes 8 errors -> 0.

.gitignore now refuses the shapes that accumulated, so a stray probe cannot
break the gate for everyone else again.

.env.example had drifted in both directions: it declared GEMINI_API_KEY, which
no code reads, and omitted eight that are read - NEXT_PUBLIC_TARGET_LANG,
NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL, and the HUGGINGFACE_*/GROQ_*/OPENROUTER_* model overrides.
The provider vars are reached through string arguments in providers.ts rather
than `process.env.X`, so a naive grep misses them; the file now matches the
real chain (huggingface -> groq -> openrouter -> groq-fallback ->
huggingface-fallback) and says out loud that those quotas are shared free tier.
